Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "there was something near the bottom of the screen, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The large, prominent “Continue Shopping” bar positioned below the Payment Details section and above the “Place Order” bar.

B) The lighter “Place Order” bar near the bottom, placed underneath the more prominent “Continue Shopping” bar.

C) The small terms and privacy policy text at the very bottom of the screen, beneath the two action-looking bars.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably B? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: What kind of situation would bring you to review an order screen where “Continue Shopping” appears more prominent than the lighter “Place Order” bar?
turns.a: I'm not sure I have one specific moment in mind. It's more of a... recurring thing, I suppose. When the team needs to process something quickly and there's not much time for setup. Though I'm not sure that's specific enough.

turns.q: When you noticed the lighter “Place Order” bar sitting below the stronger “Continue Shopping” bar, what were you trying to verify about the order screen’s layout or priorities?
turns.a: I suppose just... complete the transaction. Get it submitted. I don't usually think of it as a 'job' — it's more like a step in something larger. Someone else usually handles the follow-up.

turns.q: If this layout were redesigned, what should the bottom area make visually obvious about “Place Order” compared with “Continue Shopping”?
turns.a: The problem is visibility, really. The button to submit — the 'Place Order' button — didn't look like a primary action. It looked like a label. So I spent time looking for something that was already there, just... not visible enough.

turns.q: What visual signal would make the lighter “Place Order” bar feel like the primary order-submission action rather than secondary to “Continue Shopping”?
turns.a: The button was gray on a gray background with very small text — 12 pixels, I think. For the primary action on the screen, that's basically invisible. I couldn't tell if it was meant to be interactive, if it was disabled, or if I was just overlooking it. The barrier is the contrast. To remove it: give the 'Place Order' button a solid fill color that actually stands out from the background, and increase the text to something legible — 16 pixels minimum. That's the change. Everything else on the screen was fine.

turns.q: When you look at the lighter “Place Order” bar itself, is the problem that it has no solid fill, that the color is too light, or that the contrast against the background is too weak?
turns.a: "A filled button — solid color background, not gray, not a ghost outline. White text on a brand color, or dark text on a light fill — whatever gives you readable contrast. Something that registers immediately as 'this is interactive, this is what I press.' Right now it doesn't register as that at all. That's the only fix needed."

missed_unlock_opportunities: At turn 3, the participant referenced handing off follow-up to someone else, which implied a workflow dependency that was never explored — asking who that person was and what they needed from the submitted order could have surfaced a deeper motivational layer.

At turn 4, the participant described wasting time searching for the button, but the interviewer did not probe the emotional or cognitive cost of that delay — an opportunity was missed to unlock whether the confusion created doubt about the system's reliability or their own competence.

Across turns 3 and 4, the participant's repeated framing around speed and time pressure suggested an underlying value around efficiency or accountability that was never directly named or confirmed as a terminal value.
deflection_patterns_uncountered: The participant consistently framed responses in procedural terms ('complete the transaction', 'submit the order') without being redirected toward the personal or organizational stakes behind those actions.

Vague temporal language such as 'not much time' and 'moving on' was accepted at face value across multiple turns rather than being pressed for specificity about what was at risk if the task was delayed.
judge_report.overall_assessment: The interview made steady but slow progress toward the core barrier, with the interviewer relying on confirmatory probes in the middle turns rather than escalating toward values-level inquiry. The session ultimately identified the concrete usability barrier but did not reach a terminal value, leaving the motivational context of the participant's urgency unexplored.
